newsitem.title: UK: LME metals mostly choppy, but copper quiet in PM.
newsitem.headline: LME metals mostly choppy, but copper quiet in PM.

text.p: Copper was subdued and rangebound in the afternoon trading session on Wednesday while other base metals on the London Metal Exchange (LME) proved more erratic.
Flagship three months copper ended at $2,267 per tonne, off $11 from Tuesday's close but up sharply from a $2,247 early low.
The metal found good support around $2,250 after tumbling in the pre-market following a sizeable 17,025-tonne rise in LME stocks -- the market's most distinctive feature.
"Copper was confined to the mid-$2,260s in the afternoon, digesting movements of the past few days. It was also overshadowed by action in the other metals," a trader said.
The cash to three months backwardation shrank to $185/$195 from $200 in the morning and a high of $270 on Tuesday.

The stock rise played a big part in taming the backwardation and inventory movements over the next few days would be watched very closely, with many traders saying they expected more increases in coming days.
Aluminium found a late surge of energy in the afternoon and zoomed up to close $7 firmer at $1,570, after initially coming lower with copper in early trading.
Zinc prices was also buoyant, at one point during the afternoon rings re-hurdling the key $1,500 level initially attained on Monday.
But it was sold back down again and prices finished just $3 firmer at $1,494.
Tin and nickel, blasted by fund liquidation and stop-loss selling earlier in the day, finished near lows.
Tin crumbled through recent support around $5,500 and dropped to a nadir of $5,430, making a fresh 2-1/3 year low.
It ended just above that at $5,450, a $65 decline.
Nickel similarly sank to $6,720, the lowest level since January 10, during a midday selling binge.
It barely recovered from the lows by the end of the kerb, wrapping up $125 lower at $6,750.
Lead was $6 lower at $632, following steep losses earlier this week from Monday's high of $674.50.
It may have done enough on the downside for now, analysts said, but it remained vulnerable to downside pressure as long as it was below $650.
Alloy benefited from aluminium's bounce and was indicated firmer at $1,423/$1,428 at kerb's end.
